searchIndex.title: Introduction
searchIndex.text: This book is NOT the story of a visionary CEO, Phally Phoeurn, or of the company he founded, VP.Start. Needless to say, these two stories play a big role in the book of course, but that is not the point of this book , not really. This book is about the only person that really matters to you: You. You have a SIMA Journey. S tory, I deology, M ethodology, A mazing Innovations. You have your own distinctive STORY, you have developed your own IDEOLOGY, you plan and navigate with your own METHODOLOGY and, therefore, you too will undoubtedly create your own AMAZING INNOVATIONS. Innovations that belong to you , come from you and that could only be innovated by you. This book will introduce the SIMA Journey of VP.Start and of CEO Phally, but only as a way to help you unlock the amazing innovator that you were born to be. Nothing more and nothing less. 11 9 Let’s start with the conclusion… In Cambodian (and indeed, Asian) culture, the 12 year cycle is a very important concept. Going through 12 years indicates going through a variety of ups and downs, surviving challenges, embracing successes, pursuing opportunities and demonstrating resilience when faced with obstacles. Completing one cycle. Returning to the starting point. A time to look at where we have been and to strategize about where we want to go. 12

searchIndex.title: 2014 (Year of the Horse) VP
searchIndex.text: 2014 (Year of the Horse) VP.Start rushes onto the scene with a team of 3 family members, no branding, no customers, no equipment, no production line, no products or prototypes, no powerful connections, no name recognition, no funding, no materials or tools and no supporters. Crammed into a tiny rented space. It doesn’t sound like an auspicious starting point, does it? In fact, to be brutally honest, the nascent VP.Start team had almost nothing. But as Phally likes to say, “Having almost nothing means having something.” They had nothing EXCEPT big dreams, bold, arrogant, impossible dreams . Dreams of transforming the entire electric grid of Cambodia, making it more reliable, dependable and data-driven, and like a rushing horse, they were ready for action and ready to take risks to make their dreams comes true. Success seemed impossible at this point but to quote Phally once again, “No transformation ever happens UNTIL we try to accomplish the impossible.” 13 2015 (Year of the Goat) The year of the goat is usually considered a gentle, peaceful and harmonious year. VP.Start began its first year as a registered company. They were now an official start-up company and ready to push forward with a very powerful start. They began testing their flagship product for grid modernization, the DRC 001. Lack of space, lack of tools and lack of customers could not slow down or dampen their enthusiasm. Long nights, working weekends, low pay and an uncertain future did not deter them, either. Like a gentle and harmonious goat, they protected each other , encouraged each other and gave each other emotional support. In this year, VP.Start began its relationship with their first customers, the Cambodian utilities, namely the EDC (Electricite Du Cambodge), selling their first prototypes and getting their first serious income. Amazingly, the EDC took on the products of VP.Start before they were even developed . They could see the passion and intensity and dedication of the team and the creativity and innovation of the ideas so they decided to become customers and active supporters. This is the power of innovation. It brings to life what was only a dream. 14

searchIndex.title: 2016 (Year of the Monkey) The year of the monkey is traditionally associated with bold action and clever maneuvering but it can also become chaotic year if we are not careful
searchIndex.text: It gives people enough confidence in what is to come that they can support it along the way. Through VP.Start , the EDC saw the future of innovation. Through the EDC , VP.Start took its first baby steps towards viability as a company. Even from this earliest stage, VP.Start was already an idea-driven rather than a product-driven company. Long before they had achieved fully developed products, their ideas and voice were persuasive. The EDC and other customers bought into these ideas. They saw the power of data-driven technology and jumped on the bandwagon. | 2016 (Year of the Monkey) The year of the monkey is traditionally associated with bold action and clever maneuvering but it can also become chaotic year if we are not careful. With some revenue in hand for the first time and with some business success in the previous year, VP.Start was now ready to begin seeking opportunities, learning fast, failing fast , moving quickly and with agility, much like the monkey that represents this year. The DRC series was expanded to make the plug and play solutions work with other parts of the electric grid infrastructure and with the products of other infrastructure providers. The idea was to create a method of grid modernization that was easy to install, 15 simple to manage and quite inexpensive for a developing country with a limited budget like Cambodia. Instead of rebuilding the existing infrastructure from scratch, VP.Start was proposing a radical new approach that would take advantage of the existing infrastructure while upgrading it into a data-driven smart grid. The DRC ecosolutions would be connected to the RPM Grid which would allow for monitoring and real-time management of the electric grid, acquisition of grid data for continually upgrading the processes, clear and easy to understand visualization of grid data and the ability to find and handle anomalies and power outages remotely . Not bad for the third year of existence! Simultaneously, it was becoming clear that VP.Start was going to need more team members, more sophisticated tools, a more developed production line with increased testing and quality control. MORE! In other words, VP.Start was growing exponentially and its workspace needed to grow as well. The various constraints of space, personnel and revenue threatened to become a bottleneck that would slow growth and limit success. VP.Start was not about to let that happen! 16

searchIndex.title: 2017 (Year of the Rooster) VP
searchIndex.text: 2017 (Year of the Rooster) VP.Start entered their fourth year ready to raise their voice and shout to the heavens, like a rooster in the early morning, a scene so familiar in Cambodia. The time to hold back was past. VP.Start began hiring more team members , buying new equipment, expanding research and development, production, testing and quality control, all at the same time. This was no easy task organizationally and at times, there were problems, disagreements and confusion. It was a time for straight-talking and honest, constructive criticism. Most importantly, it was a time of self-criticism and introspection and growth. The DRC line of ecosolutions was expanded to 7 models, each designed to work with the heterogeneous products imported from various public companies that were already in use in the infrastructure of the Cambodian electric grid. The grid was becoming smarter, more affordable for consumers, less wasteful for utilities and power outages, which had long been a bane of the Cambodian economy and a drag on investment. Power outages and blackouts were being reduced BOTH in frequency and duration. At this time, a more robust grid allowed the VP.Start management team to begin to consider new ways to take full advantage of the 17 strengthened grid. One concept that came out in this year was the UCN (Universal Connectivity Network), called AlienCheck, which was an overarching connectivity app that would also allow for remote monitoring and management of home automation and IoT devices as well as the overall power management system. To many outside observers, this may have seemed like a crazy idea. Why consider creating the UCN in the middle of the monumental task of modernizing the grid? However, the VP.Start philosophy is quite direct and simple on this point. If it is a good idea that meets the needs of people, start working on it. Don’t wait. Don’t delay. Don’t hesitate. Don’t overthink. Try fast, fail faster so you can succeed fastest of all. 2018 (Year of the Dog) The dog is considered a loyal, obedient and honest animal. In this year, VP.Start continued to expand its business missions and extend its vision into new areas with honesty and integrity. The idea of smart grid modernization, energy transition and the UCN came together in one overarching framework in this year, the SIMA Journey . The SIMA (Story, Ideology, Methodology and Amazing Innovation) Journey meant that all of VP.Start’s plans, projects and products were just different aspects of one big picture journey, the journey to a more sustainable world . This SIMA Journey framework helped clarify the vision of VP.Start and 18

searchIndex.title: 2019 (Year of the Pig) The year of the pig is considered a lucky year and a year of success
searchIndex.text: ensure that all team members were on the same page. In this year, sadly, loyalty and faithfulness became problems. As a dog is faithful to his master, most of the team started to move in fidelity with the VP.Start vision and the SIMA Journey, but to be frank and candid, when a company begins transformation and growth , there are always those who don’t want to grow and transform themselves. This is true in every company experiencing powerful transformation and VP.Start was no different. Some team members started to leave VP.Start and then to speak ill of and slander the team. Some even tried to start their own business, using code and proprietary information that they stole from VP.Start. It could have been a death blow to a young, upstart company but it had the opposite effect. It brought the team together and helped to further clarify the importance of their mission. As Phally put it, “In times of transformation, negative people must leave to make space for people who want to grow.” He also stated, “Negative people don’t leave because we are on the wrong track. They leave because we are moving powerfully on the right track.” In a year that some team members left, the SIMA Journey did not stop. In fact, it picked up momentum. 19 2019 (Year of the Pig) The year of the pig is considered a lucky year and a year of success. In like fashion, VP.Start continued to make exponential growth in ideas and plans. The DRC series of products had reached over 10 models and its adoption by the EDC and various electric licensees continued apace. But this year was about more than just developing products, expanding market access and reaching new customers. Just as importantly, this was a year of charitable activities. VP.Start was founded with a mindset of generosity and compassion . Innovation through technology was implemented to make life better for people , much more than for the purpose of gaining revenue and garnering massive profits. Profits were the side benefit of creating a more sustainable Cambodia. First and foremost, grid modernization is about making a Cambodia where factories and companies can reach deadlines without electricity interruptions, students can use computers and WiFi for research without difficulties and home life can be comfortable because of dependable electricity. Innovation is a mindset and the core of the mindset is charity and concern for others. From this mindset, it was only natural for VP.Start to invest part of its profits in projects to help underprivileged students and underserved schools. This was not about building a brand or gaining a reputation 20

searchIndex.title: 2020 (Year of the Rat) In traditional thought, the year of the rat is a year of survival and adaptability
searchIndex.text: as an ethical and responsible company. This was about being true to their mindset by expressing their care and concern for their fellow Cambodians. As the profit margin of VP.Start continued to improve, the management team saw this as a perfect opportunity to use some of this profit to help others. After all, what could be more appropriate in VP.Start’s year of success than an attitude of generosity and sharing the wealth with the less fortunate? 2020 (Year of the Rat) In traditional thought, the year of the rat is a year of survival and adaptability. This was, of course, the year that Covid-19 took center stage and dominated economic development. This was a major challenge for VP.Start as indeed it was for all businesses. On the other hand, for VP.Start, this was also an opportunity to develop remote working, online connectivity and to reduce direct physical contact. Furthermore, it was also a time to solidify the teamwork that made VP.Start strong and to crystalize the gains that had been made. The management team came to recognize the value of decentralized management as Covid made highly centralized management almost impossible. While this was a year of challenges, it was also a year of significant milestones . Revenue for the year surpassed $1,000,000 US for the first time. 21 While VP.Start has never been a company to focus excessively on the financials, this was a further indication that they were headed in the right direction and that they needed to redouble their efforts by adding new team members with a variety of skills from programming to marketing, research and development to human resources, and for the f irst time, international liaison specialists . The growth of VP.Start and the needs of developing countries in the ASEAN region was convincing the leadership that the time was approaching to start thinking seriously about expanding to the global stage . 2021 (Year of the Ox) The ox is a hardworking animal, suited to harsh conditions, intense labor and slow, steady progress. This year, VP.Start had to overcome a number of serious challenges and obstacles to achieving their ultimate goals. First of all, despite seeking outside investment from banking institutions and private investors, no support was forthcoming. VP.Start revenue remained consistent and growth remained strong but outside investment was required to get VP.Start to the next level and potential investors were still uncertain about supporting the SIMA Journey vision. Secondly, the Cambodian economy (and the world economy) 22

searchIndex.title: 2022 (Year of the Tiger) As you might expect, the year of the tiger is a time of power, energy and volatility
searchIndex.text: were still struggling to recover from the ongoing effects of the Covid crisis. This might not seem like the best time, perhaps, to start a new mission or to move into a new campus or to hire a number of new team members. But as Phally likes to say, “If not now, when? If not here, where? If not us, who?” With this positive thinking powering VP.Start, it was time to expand the SIMA Journey into IoT devices and home automation and then connect them to the UCN. It was time to hire more qualified staff and increase salaries to retain quality workers. It was time to move to a brand new campus, the Sen Sok Valley Campus, with greatly expanded space, equipment, infrastructure and meeting rooms. It might not have been the best time to start all of these things but as the Tale of Two Cities famously puts it, “It was the best of times. It was the worst of times.” Or as Nikola Tesla put it, “There is no right time. There is only right now!” Phally would probably add that now is the ONLY time . We don’t know what tomorrow brings so we had better do what we can today. 2022 (Year of the Tiger) As you might expect, the year of the tiger is a time of power, energy and volatility. For VP.Start, it was a time of successes and failures, victories and frustrations. 23 This year brought in another piece of the SIMA Journey puzzle, the Smart City initiatives . Urban life in Cambodia (and most of the developing world) carried many challenges such as ineffective waste management, poor traffic systems and frequent traffic jams, inadequate parking, inefficient street lighting and so on. VP.Start decided to use data-driven technology to face these problems head on . On the less positive side, it became clear that VP.Start was not reaching its productivity goals and was in need of some dramatic changes to product development, the production line, testing, quality control and other aspects of business operations. This would test the resilience of the VP.Start team and some members would depart. VP.Start entered a period of revamping and restructuring . That said, product sales and profits continued to soar and VP.Start reached a new level of success financially. Also, for the first time, VP.Start was starting to become a known quantity in growing circles in Cambodia. No longer a start-up or even a small enterprise, VP.Start was starting to develop its own distinctive branding and name recognition. 24

searchIndex.title: 2023 (Year of the Rabbit) Traditionally, the year of the rabbit is a year for building peaceful relationships and for VP
searchIndex.text: 2023 (Year of the Rabbit) Traditionally, the year of the rabbit is a year for building peaceful relationships and for VP.Start, this meant growing connections with high schools and universities where Phally and the team held frequent workshops to encourage young people to pursue their dreams and become innovators. This also meant increasing connections with government ministries which had become aware of VP.Start’s groundbreaking work. In addition, it meant more relationships with various stakeholders and supporters who were excited about what VP.Start had already accomplished and what VP.Start was looking to accomplish in the future. There was even a burgeoning connectivity with other players in the tech sector and in other sectors of the economy, such as law enforcement and agriculture, for two examples. For the first time, there were limited connections with fellow ASEAN countries and interest in the possibilities of potential collaborative opportunities for joint ventures and pilot projects. It was still in the nascent stage at this point but VP.Start was beginning to become more than just a local company . 25 2024 (The Year of the Dragon) This year, as you might expect from a dragon, is high energy, ambitious, full of big visions and bold risks. VP.Start followed this pattern quite closely. By this point, VP.Start was rapidly approaching a team of 100 members, divided into various departments in the company hierarchy but still with a high degree of decentralization. The number of DRC models had reached 20 and were now installed in all the provinces of Cambodia, delivering a much more reliable electric grid, where power outages had become infrequent and were handled rapidly and remotely. The effects of grid modernization were even starting to become clear to consumers. Furthermore, Cambodia had become more attractive to direct foreign investment . While grid modernization was scaling up , the smart city initiative was ramping up with a pilot project In TaKhmau City, a suburb of Phnom Penh, for data-driven street lighting with IoT sensors and infrastructure. As a result, for the first time, VP.Start was able to gain some financial stability. This was also a year of increased global connections with VP.Start participating in ASEAN committee meetings and welcoming students from the Philippines and 26

searchIndex.title: 2025 (Year of the Snake) The year of the snake is traditionally associated with wise, long-term planning
searchIndex.text: tech professionals from Myanmar to the Sen Sok Campus to give them a first hand view of what they were doing and planning. This was also a year when there was a concerted effort to raise the “voice” of VP.Start, especially that of the CEO, to a new level in English and world-class communication. There could be no global VP.Start without a global voice . And as Einstein said, CEO Phally had long before determined to “be a voice, not an echo.” Not an echo of others, not even an echo of his own previous successes. Every day was a new transformative day. 2025 (Year of the Snake) The year of the snake is traditionally associated with wise, long-term planning. This was the year that the plan to access the global market started to come together. There were business trips to China, Indonesia, Singapore and pilot projects established in Malaysia and southern India. There were visits from tech executives and utility officials from Japan, South Korea, various ASEAN countries and France. Students from the University of Louisville in America visited the VP.Start campus to get caught up on the latest trends in technology. VP.Start participated in pitching trips for investment to Taiwan and Germany. Potential connections and collaborations with Bangladesh, Laos, Myanmar, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia 27 and Japan were explored as well. Sen Sok Valley changed from being a backwater to being an emerging hub in the tech scene. Plans were put in place to outsource the production line as the goal was now to scale up to more than 1 million DRC devices. VP.Start’s big ask was now $100 million US in unsecured business loans although as Phally pointed out, “This amount is just to get the ball rolling. Soon we will need 10 times that amount.” There were rapid developments in the 4 key missions of VP.Start: The SIMA Smart Grid, The SIMA Smart City, The SIMA Smart Home and the UCN and a new mission was added, SIMA Big Data , to tie all the missions together in one single journey. There were still problems at times, of course. One of the biggest issues for both international stakeholders and even local Cambodian potential supporters and investors was a deeply rooted bias against Cambodia and Cambodian companies. When Phally would make the case for innovation, people would be greatly impressed but often say things like, “Are you really Cambodian? I have never met a Cambodian like you before. You should have been born in Silicon Valley.” On the contrary, Phally would jokingly respond. “Steve Jobs should have been born in Cambodia.” 28

searchIndex.title: 2026 (Year of the Horse) Having finished the first 12 year cycle of VP
searchIndex.text: This year was the year to start raising up what Phally called “the new Angkorian generation.” As any visitor to Angkor Wat can tell you, ancient Khmer people were extremely innovative in architecture, design, sculpture, landscaping, irrigation and urban planning. The goal for VP.Start has never been to create an innovative culture from scratch but to revive the creative spirit that has always be a key aspect of Khmer culture . 2026 (Year of the Horse) Having finished the first 12 year cycle of VP.Start, the VP.Start team is faced with a serious question. What comes in the next cycle? It is still quite early but some trends are obvious already. More rapid growth, especially with the imminent rollout of the UCN and rapidly increasing demand for pilot projects throughout ASEAN and South Asia in the smart grid, smart city and smart home initiatives. More intense globalisation as VP.Start begins to spread outside of Cambodia. More development of a true smart grid in Cambodia. Currently some 80% of the grid in Cambodia remains conventional, but more than 1,000,000 DRC devices will dramatically change that. More expansion in hiring team members and in enlarging 29 the Sen Sok Campus. More explosive, exponential growth and even greater ROI. Revenue of $100 million or more in the next 5 to 6 years based on traction estimates. And yes, there will be problems. There always are. But as Jensen Huang has put it wisely, “Greatness comes from character. And character isn’t formed out of smart people. It’s formed out of people who have suffered.” What is the soul of the next 12 years for VP.Start? Transformation. In a word, transformation. VP.Start is poised to become a true unicorn, a major player on the global stage, a leader in innovation through technology, while never forgetting its roots and heritage and never stopping its generous, charitable activities. VP.Start is out to change the world, make it more sustainable and build a brighter future. Nothing less will do. No stopping or slowing down until the goal is achieved! 30

searchIndex.text: The VP.Start team believes that success comes from knowing your story. Facing your story, successes and faults. Admitting your story and owning your story. Being proud of your story, even the flaws, because they also brought you to this point. There are valuable lessons to be learned in your story and mine. But we will never start to learn those lessons and gain those valuable insights, until we accept our story as it is. Every story has a beginning. Often the start of a story sets the trajectory for the whole story. Where did your story start? What does that start teach you? Did you make a Very Powerful (VP) Start? 37 38

searchIndex.title: Pages 39-40
Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin
searchIndex.text: Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin.” -Tony Robbins How do you begin the journey of innovation? The SIMA Journey of Innovation through Technology did not start out in a big city. Not in a famous educational institution. Not in an affluent suburb. Not with a lot of excitement. Not with expectation. The road to VP.Start and innovation started, as journeys often do, with hardship. But if “Necessity is the mother of invention” , then “Hardship is def initely the mother of innovation.” Buddha himself, whom many Cambodians would consider the ultimate innovator, according to the traditional stories, was just an ordinary prince until he stepped outside the palace gates and saw the sufferings and hardship in the world. Hardship made him an enlightened innovator. This is the mindset that a young boy named Phally was raised in. Or actually, he was not named Phally. He was not named at all. What are the ingredients required to make a successful innovator? 41 The boy, growing up in a dirt poor village, living in a simple handmade hut, waking up and sleeping early in rhythm with the sunrise and sunset, candles instead of electricity, rainwater instead of running water, living through the after effects of the disastrous Pol Pot era. No medicine, no transportation, almost no education. Not exactly the ideal conditions to raise up a future innovator. But one thing had survived the cataclysm of the civil war, the Khmer Rouge and the Vietnamese invasion. Family. Family was the foundation that kept Cambodia from becoming another failed state. As long as there was family, there was hope. What is your name and how do you add value to that name? The as yet unnamed boy was blessed with a loving, caring mother and a wise and somewhat unique father. A father who decided not to give his son a name. Education was very intermittent but the father insisted on his boy going to school whenever possible. On the first day of school, the teacher asked the boy his name. “I don’t know. I don’t think I have one,” was the boy’s response. The boy ran home and asked his father, “What is my name?” The father smiled wryly and said, 42

searchIndex.title: Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin
searchIndex.text: “That is for you to choose. In this world, we must make our own name. ” The boy thought for a second and said, “Phally.” “OK, Phally, it is, my son.” As Phally was still 3 years old and unable to write in Khmer, he had his older sister write out his name for him. Now it was official. The father insisted that Phally was unique from that very young age. He told Phally to follow his dreams and never care what others thought of him. Those lessons are still playing out today. In other words, Phally didn’t become a revolutionary innovator and a champion of Big Data, grid modernization and the power of creativity to overcome even the darkest situations overnight . Or maybe he did. The story of Phally’s childhood is not told to say he was perfect by any means. Phally is no saint and he can be notoriously hard to deal with . As a small child and now as well. Of course, true innovators often are hard to deal with . But then again, not every person who is hard to deal with , is a true innovator, of course. I will allow the reader to pass their own judgment on such questions. Why is it so hard for most of us to “be ourselves”? How do we become the innovators that we should be 43 without becoming “hard to deal with”? When Phally was a teenager, it became clear that he was in many ways atypical. He followed his own pattern , marched to the beat of a drum that only he could hear and didn’t mind telling classmates, older kids and even teachers exactly what he thought… and at times, why they were wrong ! In Cambodia, this was NOT and is still NOT done! But Phally’s father had told him that he was not to care what others said of him or thought of him. And he took it to heart with true intensity. His classmates quickly gave him the nickname of “alien” because he didn’t seem to be from the same planet as the rest of them. But perhaps, it wasn’t so much his unique philosophies that “alienated” him, if you will, as much as the matter of fact way in which he would tell his perspectives. Years later, when meeting with much older CEOs of companies much larger, more famous and with more storied histories than VP.Start, Phally never hesitated to tell his much more experienced and wealthier counterparts to stop his wasting time, get to the point and focus on the big picture. He would tell them that they might have manufacturing skills, 44

searchIndex.title: Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin
searchIndex.text: engineering prowess and substantial revenue but he had something that they did not possess and that they desperately needed: his creativity. Furthermore, he had the compelling voice that they lacked. You might expect that these CEOs in their fancy suits with big offices and matching titles and first class airplane seats would take offense at this upstart daring to call them out to their faces. You would think that if you didn’t know the unique charm of this “alien”, the charm that worked wonders on his classmates and teachers long before it was deployed against state of the art, cutting edge, groundbreaking, jargon spewing CEOs. Phally was in middle school, which for a lot of students of Phally’s generation, was as far as they got in education, or indeed, farther than many of them got. It was time for the math exam. Students came into the sweaty classroom, fans occasionally pushing the hot air around, sweating from equal parts of the oppressive heat and the exam pressures. The teacher was solemn and unsmiling. The teacher was deeply concerned about this batch of students. The time allotted was 90 minutes. Just as the exam was about to begin, Phally made his entrance. After 15 minutes, Phally turned in his exam paper. Some classmates might have wrongly guessed that he had given up on the test, 45 but in fact, he had completed the test without an error. To tell the truth, Phally was utterly unconcerned about his exam scores or about being the top student in the class or any similar honors. He was just happy to see his classmates succeed and he worked hard to tutor them in his free time, to help them all improve. Students even came from other classes and classrooms, climbing in the windows, to be tutored by Phally. Either way, that was not the feat, that burned the “alien” image indelibly into everyone’s collective memory. The teacher told Phally that he must sit down and wait until the end of the exam period to turn in his exam. Turning the exam in too early might make the other students uncomfortable and give them some added pressure. Phally wasn’t buying it. “Why should I be penalized to make other students feel more comfortable?” Phally began his bold response to his teacher. “Why do I need to sit and waste 75 minutes of my life to take the pressure off others? They need more pressure, not less.” Not surprisingly, teachers were not to be talked back to in this fashion. And yet, somehow, as always, Phally managed to coax a grin out of his teacher. Almost inexplicably, actions and behaviors that would get anyone else in a world of trouble, never seemed to put the “alien” in much of a bind at all. Perhaps, it was the unabashed certainty of the words, the pure and honest sincerity or 46

searchIndex.title: Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin
searchIndex.text: just an inability on the part of the teacher not to feel a little respect for the chutzpah of this young student. Teachers and classmates might not appreciate his attitude at times but it was hard to look at young Phally and not think that there was something different here, that they were privy to witnessing the childhood of someone who would become many things but never become boring. Phally was not through speaking yet. Not only, he insisted, was he not to be punished for finishing early. As a matter of fact, quite the opposite, he should be rewarded. If he could get a perfect score in 15 minutes, how could that be the same score as someone who achieved the feat in 90 minutes? He was calling for a deduction in the scores of students who could not keep up with him. He didn’t want to share perfect marks with others who took longer to achieve what he accomplished so quickly and effortlessly. This is a core perspective of VP.Start. It is insufficient and inadequate to merely achieve great outcomes and great innovations. VP.Start must achieve them more quickly than anyone else. Speed is just as important as accuracy. If you can achieve greater results faster than others without sacrificing quality or accuracy, you will be able to achieve amazing innovations. How about you? Are you dedicated to achieving your ideas in the least possible time but without sacrificing accuracy? Once again, in a normal world, 47 you would likely expect that students would not appreciate someone trying to reduce their scores to benefit his own, just because they used the entire allotted time. And yet, his classmates had come to know and love “the alien,” just as his teacher had and just as future CEOs and government officials would come to. This brings up a few of the key points of Phally’s philosophy that emerge from his story, his background. How can we accomplish our tasks more efficiently and substantiate this efficiency? First, for Phally and VP.Start, it is not enough to do things right. You must do them as rapidly and efficiently as possible as well. A successful result achieved in half a year is more valuable than a similar result achieved in two years. Even before he knew the meaning of the term, he was data-driven, constantly pushing to upgrade himself and others, never willing to be satisfied. What makes you unique and how can you foster and cultivate that uniqueness? Secondly, he had and still has the view of himself as someone distinctive, someone special and unique. This did not spring from his pride or overconfidence but from experience. He could do things well, learn things quickly and make connections that others did not see. As one example of that, at one point, 48

searchIndex.title: Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin
searchIndex.text: Phally was, like so many of us, a struggling math student, failing to see the point or the purpose behind the equations. He had fallen considerably behind his classmates and his math teacher had even begun to express concern to his parents. Yet, it was a motivational issue rather than any inability to do the work. He felt no need to do math and couldn’t seem to get why he had to waste his “valuable” time on such pursuits. He would much rather feed the chickens and raise vegetables and earn money in the local market to support his family. He certainly wasn’t concerned about grades or scores or his ranking relative to others. But one day, at the age of 10, it suddenly dawned on him. The philosophy underpinning math. The way that math was a logic system. The way that math attempted to bring the universe into focus. It was as much as moment of spiritual intuition as a moment of academic development. Suddenly, he roared into action, mastering everything that the teacher could give him and exploding into the top rank in his class, working on university level math at age 11 and 12. What is limiting and hindering your exponential growth? How will you remove those obstacles? Interestingly, and in keeping with his very nature, he tells this story often but never to brag. He often says that accomplishments are best forgotten so that they don’t hinder us from taking the next step. He mentions this story because he believes that this is exponential growth that WE ALL are capable of. 49 Once we have that moment of inspiration, that moment of clarity, we are all capable of almost superhuman feats of academic development overnight. Any failure of growth is not a failure of ability or potential. It is merely a failure of insight . “If you know why you live, you will know how to live and what living is.” It goes without saying that this philosophy puts pressure on his team. But to be fair, Phally puts more pressure on himself than on anyone else. Always frustrated, but never discouraged. Always unsatisf ied, but never hopeless. “The day that I don’t want the impossible and stop feeling frustrated, f ind a new CEO!” You might say that Phally was an innovator from birth. And yet, while seeing himself as unique, he was clear that everyone was distinctive and amazing ; the main difference was most people did not have the courage to be the amazing innovators that they were by nature. They were afraid to unlock themselves , step outside the box and they allowed school, peer pressure, family and societal expectations, stirred up in some oppressive cocktail, to compromise and customize them, to keep them from reaching their ultimate goal. To reach the unreachable star. To be freely and completely yourself. Phally might be many things at different times 50

searchIndex.title: Chapter 1 The SIMA Story The Journey of a Thousand Miles Begins “The only impossible journey is the one that you never begin
searchIndex.text: but there was one thing that he always was without hesitation or exception. Himself. This didn’t always make him the easiest to understand, the easiest to deal with or the easiest to get a handle on. But it made him what he was and still is. It is his occasionally irritating but always irresistible charm. His charisma. His innovative nature. How do we unlearn the toxic trait of caring too much about what others think? One other characteristic that emerged from this period of Phally’s life was his complete disregard for titles, positions, awards and all the trappings of modern success, including financial gain. If you don’t care what others think of you, what do their awards and certif ications mean to you? What good is a title like CEO or COO if you can’t hold down or live up to the title of Innovator , the only title that really matters? What does it really mean to have a high position and experience and accolades? Just because you may have worked more years or earned more money or sold more products , according to Phally, that certainly does not indicate that 51 you have accomplished more . More experience could merely mean more experience of doing things the wrong way or at least, in a less effective way. The only award that matters to Phally is knowing that he had served the cause of innovation without fear. So, at this point, Phally wants to ask you a question……. How about you? Are you willing to take on the challenge of being the innovator that you were born to be? Are you willing to push yourself to be better and to never be satisfied with who you are and what you have achieved? Are you willing to defy authority in the pursuit of creativity and innovation? Are you willing to maintain the focus required to keep pushing forward? Are you willing to take the greatest risk to gain the greatest reward: the thrill of being yourself ? 52

searchIndex.title: Chapter 2 The SIMA Story Learning to Learn in the SIMA Way “Self-education is, I f irmly believe, the only kind of education there is
searchIndex.text: Chapter 2 The SIMA Story Learning to Learn in the SIMA Way “Self-education is, I f irmly believe, the only kind of education there is.” -Isaac Asimov If you have read this far, you have already started to recognize some of the characteristics that make Phally who he is; complicated, disciplined, dedicated, at times infuriating, but certainly fascinating and endlessly innovative. Why is advanced education a major stepping stone towards founding VP.Start? University education was a the next key stage of the journey to VP.Start. Phally considers the ITC (the Institute of Technology of Cambodia) as his second hometown, his professors as his spiritual parents and his classmates as family. But like any family relationship, the road to innovation was not without friction. Phally loves giving presentations at universities and meeting with students and professors. He feels a special affinity that he doesn’t feel speaking in a company boardroom or at a government ministry meeting room or even at a public utility office. University is where he feels most at home because he loves to learn, to research and to delve into the most arcane details of technology. As a matter of fact, if he had not felt compelled by innovation to become a CEO, I am convinced that he could have become a very popular professor of 53 electrical engineering, perhaps with a Richard Feynman vibe. How do you learn? What is your learning style? Do you agree that “traveling 1000s of miles is more valuable than reading 1000s of books”, as the Chinese proverb proclaims? If you think that this means that Phally was a model student and that this phase of the journey to building VP.Start was easy, you would be mistaken. He was driven, possessed, quite literally consumed with learning but found it nearly impossible to focus on anything that didn’t seem “mission critical.” Each professor had to substantiate that their curriculum and textbooks were worthwhile. The onus was on squarely on the professor. Failure by the professor to do so, would mean that Phally would quickly lose interest. Phally meant no disrespect, although it was not always interpreted that way by his teachers. Phally saw himself as on a mission to change the world . He also realized the impermanence of life and the shortness of time to accomplish what he was starting to dare to dream of. There just wasn’t enough time to waste on anything less than absolutely essential. How do innovators approach education? In fact, Phally would be more likely to study things outside of the curriculum altogether than things in the textbook that he considered obsolete or inadequate. Again and perhaps not so surprisingly, some professors did not appreciate this brash attitude. 54

searchIndex.title: Chapter 2 The SIMA Story Learning to Learn in the SIMA Way “Self-education is, I f irmly believe, the only kind of education there is
searchIndex.text: But this is actually not so unusual among innovators. For example, Steve Jobs, before dropping out of school completely, would famously rush off to calligraphy classes instead of attending the classes he was required to attend. He later credited this calligraphy skill as critical in designing various Apple products. Similarly, Phally didn’t really care what others thought of him or how they chose to grade him. The important exam was life and he was going to ace that test. How he did on a test in a classroom designed by a professor didn’t concern him in the least. The real tests were designed by nature and the experiences of life. The real grades, the only marks that mattered to Phally were simple: Am I a true innovator or not? Do I have what it takes to achieve my goals? The only ranking that mattered to him was this: Am I a better creative thinker today than the Phally of yesterday? How do innovators succeed in the innovative journey without compromising? Just they did for like Steve Jobs, Einstein, and others, and fortunately for Phally and for all of us, there were some professors, mentors and supporters who saw the method in the madness of Phally and accepted him as he was. This is a lifelong, recurring pattern for Phally. While some, perhaps many, were put off by Phally’s idiosyncrasies and refusal to acquiesce to societal norms, there were and still are always a chosen few who could see the potential andvisionary nature of Phally and accept him as he is. Those supporters of Phally, I dare say, see in him just a hint of themselves or, at least, 55 a hint of whom they would like to be if they dared to be true to themselves. In the educational journey to a greater vision, where do you place your focus? While many others found university life a great time to experiment and explore socially, Phally always had his eyes on a loftier prize. His passion was creativity and his addiction was improving himself. He pursued his dreams of a brighter future for Cambodia with a single-mindedness that bordered in obsession. Later this passion would manifest itself with the creation of VP.Start. He didn’t create VP.Start because he had some entrepreneurial spirit that he needed to express through business. He was compelled to create VP.Start because he felt it was the most efficient way to achieve his dreams . More on that later…. Dating, entertainment, drinking, and other trivial pursuits were all relegated. He took on the ways of a Buddhist monk, so to speak, rejecting the pleasures of this world for a higher standard, a higher calling. Indeed, for him, the way of Innovation through Technology is a spiritual endeavour. Anything that might distract him was rejected. He was on the road to electrical enlightenment. By the way, this is not to say that Phally was opposed to either alcohol or female companionship, per se. He made a conscious, pragmatic and conscientious decision to avoid 56

searchIndex.title: Chapter 3 The SIMA Story Engineering the SIMA Revolution “Be yourself; everyone else is already taken
searchIndex.text: all attachments. In his view, life was short, ephemeral, impermanent. He had revolutionary changes to make and no time for a family to slow him down or for leisure to make him lazy . Sleep seemed a waste of time as well so he determined to get by on the minimum of sleep and exercise and to spend his energy for his one and only pursuit, a sustainable future for his country and his world. Phally wants to ask you a few more questions. What is your journey and does it outweigh everything else? What are the distractions that might hinder and hamper your journey ? And, most critically, if you don’t know what your journey is , how do you expect to reach the destination? 57 Chapter 3 The SIMA Story Engineering the SIMA Revolution “Be yourself; everyone else is already taken.” -Oscar Wilde How do we become innovators? During a panel discussion at the Royal University of Phnom Penh, a sincere student posed a question to Phally. Phally had been the keynote speaker at a conference on the power of innovation and had talked about the differences between innovation and optimisation, creativity and engineering. The student mustered up all her courage and asked Phally, “How do we become innovators?” Phally smiled. He smiles a lot. This was the perfect question that would enable him to state his philosophy succinctly and powerfully. As the audience went silent with expectation, Phally slowly replied. “If you are asking this question, you are already an innovator.” Phally looked at the student and then out to the hundreds of students gathered of their own free-will to hear a lecture about innovation. Phally continued. “To tell the truth, all of you are innovators by nature. How does a banana become a banana? How does a fish become a fish? Everyone is born to be an innovator. Innovation is the way of nature. 58

searchIndex.title: Chapter 3 The SIMA Story Engineering the SIMA Revolution “Be yourself; everyone else is already taken
searchIndex.text: Evolution is just the scientific way of expressing the innovative nature of our natural world and of the universe. You don’t need to worry about how to become an innovator any more than you need to worry about how to become a person. You are already an innovator and you were born for that very purpose. ” You were born to be an innovator. Are you living up to your birthright? Phally now posed a question back to the audience as he had transformed from a keynote speaker to more of an ascetic philosopher. “So, let me ask you something. If everyone was born to be an innovator, why are there so few innovators? Why are there so few innovative companies? Why are there so few innovations?’ The crowd went silent. Phally smiled broadly. He was in his element. “It is not because we were not born to be innovators. It is because most of us are afraid to be ourselves. Society tries to force us into a box . Parents tell us to behave. Teachers tell us to follow the rules . Companies push us to conform. They try to convince us not to be ourselves and all too often they succeed.” “But look at the true innovators. Oscar Wilde. Einstein. Socrates. Alan Turing. 59 Buddha. They broke the rules , went outside the comfort zone, refused to let the world harness them. They were disruptive, distinctive, unique and completely unafraid. The true innovators are often criticized and even punished, some even killed but they never stop being themselves. ” “The real question that we need to ask is not, ‘How do I become an innovator?’ or “How do I unlock my creativity?’ The only question is, ‘How do I become myself ?’ Phally insists on being himself. He commands that of everyone who works for VP.Start. There can be no innovative company UNLESS there is an absolute dedication to their vision, to their goals, to their dreams. To being themselves! Why is it hard yet essential for us to become ourselves? And yet, to become yourself, while it seems like the easiest thing in the world, is in fact, quite challenging. As French philosopher, Albert Camus stated, “Man is the only animal that refuses to be what it is.” You don’t need to tell a turtle or a snake or a lion to be themselves. They can never be anything else. And yet people very often choose to refuse to be who they are. And as Phally would insist in many speeches, it is a choice. We don’t refuse to become ourselves by accident or chance or circumstances. 60

searchIndex.title: Chapter 3 The SIMA Story Engineering the SIMA Revolution “Be yourself; everyone else is already taken
searchIndex.text: We actively choose to be or not to be ourselves. And we keep making that choice day after day after day. Phally, as I mentioned before and will likely mention again, was certainly no saint, no angel. Indeed, there are many faults that you might accuse Phally of. He can lose focus at times. He can be frustrated with people who don’t get him immediately. He might demand too much of others and of himself at times, pushing people beyond their limits. But there is one accusation that you could never make about Phally. You could never claim that Phally is not true to himself. He is unapologetically and unabashedly himself. F ew others could dare to claim the same. Why do true innovators often need to found new companies? Why do they often struggle in more conventional company hierarchies? Because Phally was such a firm believer in the power of innovation and in the power of being yourself, it was almost inevitable that it was not going to be easy for Phally in a traditional company. And yet, fresh out of school, Phally found himself working as an electrical engineer for a small, traditional company. He threw himself into the work and gained valuable experience. More important, perhaps, than even his experience as an engineer, he gained experience with the problems of the aging Cambodian electric grid and the negative impact it had on locals. Phally was posted to Kampong Cham province, a place he still considers his second home to this day. He was tasked with keeping the electric grid up and 61 running and responding to outages. Not surprisingly, outages often occurred in remote areas in times of bad weather. Outages didn’t usually occur at the most convenient times, either . As a result, many a midnight would find Phally on a dark, rugged road in a bad weather travelling to a remote location to try to restore power. Why do innovators often need to face problems directly before they can solve them? It was a difficult job in less than ideal conditions but Phally was excited about his work. He knew firsthand the importance of reliable electric power and the problems that developed when it was not dependable. He saw himself as a kind of hero, fighting the forces of nature and weather and time, on behalf of the beleaguered electric grid. As always, Phally remained the optimist who believed in the power of one person to make a change for good . Yet all of the optimism and positivity that Phally could muster was unable to mask some key issues that ate at Phally. First of all, the grid and its aging infrastructure were getting worse, not better, despite the best efforts of Phally and his equally dedicated colleagues. The problems that plagued the grid, causing frequent outages, problems like flooding, intense rain, extreme heat and rapid growth of vegetation were beyond his ability to combat. Furthermore, these situations were unlikely to change. As he and his team would restore power, 62

searchIndex.title: Chapter 3 The SIMA Story Engineering the SIMA Revolution “Be yourself; everyone else is already taken
searchIndex.text: he couldn’t help but be aware that he had not really solved the problem ; he had merely repaired the grid until the next outage came along. He was constantly putting bandages on broken legs . And outages were getting more, not less frequent . And lasting longer, not less time . Why do innovators often seem to feel frustrated? Does their frustration with the current situation lead them to innovative solutions? But what really frustrated Phally was that he was often called back to the same locations to do the same repairs in response to the same problems . Two steps forward and three steps back. He was working as hard as he could but seemingly without any progress. For Phally, the one thing that he cannot abide is feeling that he is making no progress . He is willing to face challenges , no matter how daunting, because he believes deeply in his ability to make an improvement. But he simply cannot tolerate a lack of progress . At this point, Phally, still a neophyte in the electrical engineering sector, began to make suggestions to his boss, suggestions of Big Picture changes, suggestions that were well beyond his experience or position or rank. Not surprisingly, I suppose, his innovative ideas were viewed as the opinions 63 of a naive kid. The questions came roaring back to Phally from the company management. Do you really think that Cambodia can modernize and transform its grid? Where is the funding coming from? Who has the technology to achieve this transformation? And, why do you think that you have all the answers that much more experienced and respected engineers have never been able to achieve? In one question, Who do you think you are? Let me ask you, as well, dear readers: Who do you think you are? That said, the management team of the company recognized his passion, his intensity and his fervor for his ideas. No one ever doubted that. Why do innovators choose revolutionary change over incremental improvements? At this point, the safe approach for Phally would be to stay in his lane, stay inside the box, follow the rules, obey his superiors and try to achieve some kind of gradual, incremental improvement of the electric grid. For most people, that would be the road that they would choose. But for Phally, that would break the most fundamental rule of all . “To be yourself.” That was the one rule that was impossible for Phally to break. 64

searchIndex.title: Chapter 3 The SIMA Story Engineering the SIMA Revolution “Be yourself; everyone else is already taken
searchIndex.text: Phally has stated many times that he never wanted to become the CEO of a tech company. He would have been far happier to be a teacher in a rural village school or a “nameless” electrician plugging away in a traditional company. He could have had a normal life with a family and a decent salary and reasonably secure future. But he was “compelled by technology to become a CEO” as he puts it. At the end of the day, he had no choice but to be himself. Phally would like to challenge you with a question or two…. Do you know yourself ? Not the self you show to the world or even the self you show to yourself. Do your know the real yourself ? Are you willing to become yourself in spite of all the risks? Phally believes that no one ever becomes a successful innovator in tech until after they become themselves . And, although it is definitely not always easy to be yourself , in the end it is a decision that you will never regret. So, are you willing to stay true to yourself , regardless of what praise or criticism may come your way? Are you ready to become the innovator that you were born to be? 65 66

searchIndex.title: Chapter 4 The SIMA Story The Birth of a Company, the Rebirth of a CEO “Should I stay or should I go? If I stay, there will be trouble
searchIndex.text: Chapter 4 The SIMA Story The Birth of a Company, the Rebirth of a CEO “Should I stay or should I go? If I stay, there will be trouble. If I go, it will be double.” -The Clash The time had come for Phally to stand up and follow his dreams. He saw the big picture, the bottlenecks facing Cambodian development. He was unwilling to accept the current situation. He was determined to transform the electric grid. Not tweak it, not upgrade it, not optimise it, not even improve it. Revolutionize the grid. Disrupt it. Transform it! He was hellbent on transforming the grid, the very nature of how electricity was distributed in Cambodia and ultimately in the world. Why is it hard for most people to make big decisions? Why do true innovators refuse to compromise or customize for others? With some sadness, he had already left his conventional job, convinced that he would never be able to achieve more than incremental upgrades of the electric grid in that position. He was a little disappointed with this outcome but he was not one to look back . He did not leave the engineering job acrimoniously. He had always felt that life was a journey and 67 people and positions were destined to come and go. When people aligned with his vision, he would go with them and they would go with him, but, at the same time, he and they were free to part ways at any time, no hard feelings. In later years, his hiring and staff retention practices at VP.Start were similarly flexible. The door is always open , he would say, open for those who share our vision to join the journey. But by the same token, the door is also open for those who had lost the vision and chosen to leave. No criticism for those who go, no excessive joy for those who come and those who stay . Everyone was free to follow THEIR dreams. Everyone needs to follow their own journey. And the time had come for Phally to start his. Another aspect of Phally’s perspective is that in his world there is no time but now. Yesterday is gone and all that remains is an illusion of the memory. Tomorrow has not yet arrived and is similarly little more than a figment of the imagination. There is only now so everything must be done immediately. After all, we don’t know if we will even be alive tomorrow. What will happen to our innovations if we start postponing them? This “living in the perpetual present” mindset means that Phally rushes in where “wise men” never go. He was ready to change the world and 68

searchIndex.title: Chapter 4 The SIMA Story The Birth of a Company, the Rebirth of a CEO “Should I stay or should I go? If I stay, there will be trouble
searchIndex.text: change it right now , to make the electric grid of Cambodia reliable, dependable, equitable, affordable and renewable. NOW. According to Phally, if you don’t do something now, you will never do it. Not next year or sometime down the road. RIGHT NOW! RIGHT AWAY! Why do innovators boldly (and perhaps foolishly) take on “impossible” challenges? Of course, there were a few rather serious obstacles in his way. First off, the electric grid was made up of aging and in some cases seriously damaged infrastructure , outages were getting more instead of less frequent , technology was far from cutting edge indeed, there was little to no foreign investment and resources to devote to grid modernization were very minimal. This would likely cause most people to give up before they started. But, to state the obvious, none of this deterred Phally in the least. Furthermore, in a society where patronage and connections were critical to business success, Phally was an outsider and an unknown , espousing ideas that seemed heretical to the electric grid orthodoxy of the day. At this point, he had a team of himself plus two relatives, working without salaries, in a tiny closet of a rented office space, working non-stop. There were no weekends, no holidays , work started before dawn and ended in the middle of the night. 69 At this time, Phally started his practice of sleeping 3 to 4 hours per night. In his view, as mentioned before, sleeping was wasting time , time that could not be recovered. And since he was trying to create a company to upend the electric grid and change the world, sleep was a luxury that he could not afford. How do you refresh yourself and alleviate the stress of innovation? The only break that Phally would allow himself were visits to the nearby Buddhist pagoda. When he was with the monks, Phally was happy to sit in silence and listen and learn, to absorb their wisdom and ideology, to meditate on what the monks shared. This is another aspect of Phally’s practice that remains to this day. No matter how busy he is or how many projects he is juggling or how many influential business or government leaders he is meeting, he always finds time to get to the pagoda. He calls it “spending to communicate with himself.” And he considers this time essential to him being an innovator. For that brief period of time, he no longer needs to be the lead actor , the revolutionary, the groundbreaker, the game changer, the rule breaker, the disrupter. He can sit at the feet of the monks and, for a moment, just be Phally, the simple boy from the rural village, studying by candlelight. In those precious moments in the pagoda with the monks, he is able to revert briefly to his childhood. He is able to be Phally, the boy who named himself, sitting, as it were, with his father , 70

searchIndex.title: Chapter 4 The SIMA Story The Birth of a Company, the Rebirth of a CEO “Should I stay or should I go? If I stay, there will be trouble
searchIndex.text: who still advises him from the next world. Recharged, he is able to leave the pagoda and rush back into the fray of making our world a better place. You and I might think that it is a bit too much to imagine a team of 3 with no experience, no name recognition, no branding, no connections, no resources, no revenue, no prospects, no backers and no realistic prospects of gaining any of these, setting out to change the world. Too naive. Too innocent. Too impossible. Too ridiculous. You and I, needless to say, are not Phally. Despite all the limitations that he faced while founding the company that would become VP.Start, he did have one powerful possession . His superpower. He was possessed with a spirit of absolute confidence in his vision. It wasn’t overconfidence, hubris or pride, in his view. Phally would argue that, on the contrary, everyone should feel that way about their dreams. It is not arrogance to believe in yourself and your journey 100%. In fact, those who did not feel that kind of “arrogance” had the problem, not those who did. His absolutely unshakable belief in himself, 71 his team and his journey was matched by another equally powerful idea. He believed and knew that Cambodia needed grid modernization desperately. Someone would surely eventually achieve grid modernization and bring Cambodia into the modern age of the global economy, so, Phally thought, why not let me be the one who achieves it? Here. Now. Me. How do innovators achieve the impossible? What lessons can we take from their unshakable belief in themselves? We often hear of the proverbial collision of the unstoppable force with the unmovable object. As they say, something has got to give. The seemingly unmovable object was the dinosaur, the aging, collapsing electric grid infrastructure of Cambodia. The unstoppable force was Phally, his team and his vision. The collision of the two was the founding of VP.Start. It is not by accident that Phally decided to name the company that he created with his tiny team, VP (Very Powerful) Start. Very Powerful Start. Phally knew that to achieve dramatic change, transformational, generational change, it was going to take a very powerful force to move that immovable object. And that company was going to have to be very powerful from the very start. How do you make a Very Powerful Start against a seemingly intractable problem? 72

searchIndex.title: Chapter 5 The Reluctant CEO “The desire to be a politician should bar you for life from ever becoming one
searchIndex.text: A conventional approach was certainly not going to provide the very powerful start that was necessary. Phally need creativity and innovation to solve the problem of grid modernization, solve it rapidly, affordably and completely. Results needed to be forthcoming quickly because he would have to build his business on the back of these results. Are you ready to face intractable problems, impossible obstacles and unbeatable dilemmas? Are you ready to tackle the immovable object? And make it move ? Are you crazy enough to try something that EVERYONE knows will fail and resilient enough to gain success against all odds? If you really believe in the power of innovation, what do you need to be afraid of? 73 Chapter 5 The Reluctant CEO “The desire to be a politician should bar you for life from ever becoming one.” -Billy Connoly, comedian If you applied this same principle to CEOs as to politicians, Phally would certainly agree. These is no greater threat to innovation than a CEO who loves his power, his position, his salary. The moment a CEO falls in love with those material successes, the CEO and the company stop growing . The rule is absolute: Grow or die ! No exceptions, no excuses, nothing more and nothing less! What is the key to becoming a successful CEO in tech? According to Phally’s view of management, the key prerequisite for becoming a successful CEO is never wanting to become one in the first place . If you start enjoying the power, the prestige, the title, the office, the perks, the salary or any other trappings of being a CEO, you are not only unsuited for the role, but you will surely cause your business to fail . A good and effective CEO must be pulled into being one almost against their will, 74

searchIndex.title: Chapter 5 The Reluctant CEO “The desire to be a politician should bar you for life from ever becoming one
searchIndex.text: drawn by the power of innovation and by their unwavering, inescapable commitment to fulfilling their vision. The CEO must have a clear vision of the future that she or he must create, a goal so crystal clear and so powerful that nothing can stand in the way, he way, not even the inconvenience of having to become a CEO in order to achieve that goal. What are your dreams leading you to do? Are you following those dreams or trying to ignore them? If Phally is to be believed and if his claims are true, he was coerced by his dreams of a sustainable future for our world into becoming a CEO when there was no other option. Despite himself. In spite of his desire to live a simple, quiet life. He knew that the electric grid must be modernized . It was the only way for Cambodia to recover from its dark and troubled past and have a bright future. He also knew that incremental change was never going to get the job done. As a matter of fact, it would probably allow the situation to deteriorate further. A revolution was required. And revolutions require revolutionaries. Phally further knew that as long as he was working in a conventional company working for a traditional boss in a typical hierarchy, he was not going to be able to effect the change that his ideas insisted on. Let me reiterate at this point that Phally adamantly and repeatedly states that he valued and appreciated his time as an electrician . It helped him develop many of the skills that he still employs today. 75 It gave him a deep understanding of the challenges that electrical engineers face and an in-depth knowledge of the limitations of the conventional grid . Phally has nothing but respect and a spirit of camaraderie and admiration for his boss and colleagues from those days, many of who he still works with in his new role. But he knew, as deeply as he knew anything, that the revolution was coming , that it had to be coming, and he had to be at the forefront of that transformation. When the time for transformation comes, are you ready to make the change? Are you prepared to take the risk? So, how does an unknown “CEO” of a barely functioning company with no name recognition, no track record and no connections take his ideas and his prototype product to the EDC, the electrical utility of Cambodia? With a lot of bravery, courage and, perhaps, a bit of blissful ignorance of just how impossible and quixotic his quest was. “Fortune favors the bold.” -Ancient Roman proverb How do you do what you know you MUST do even though it seems impossible to do it? Better question still, how does a CEO of an unregistered company persuade utilities and other customers to buy the beta version of his product, while he is still developing the final version and while he is simultaneously implementing it and 76

searchIndex.title: Chapter 5 The Reluctant CEO “The desire to be a politician should bar you for life from ever becoming one
searchIndex.text: gradually expanding it throughout the entire grid system of Cambodia. We have already spoken of authenticity , being yourself. We have spoken of brash confidence in the face of daunting challenges. These are surely critical factors in the success of the SIMA Journey and your journey , too. But there is another factor that may even go further to explain the inexplicable. The crazy success of VP.Start despite all the odds against it. Absolute commitment, dedication, faithfulness. Passion bordering on obsession or addiction. Something you show rather than say. Something that people see and cannot deny. A person can be authentic and still be authentically incompetent . A person can be hyperconfident even though they have no logical right to be so. But to have absolute, untouchable commitment , that comes from a different place. Of course, you can be dedicated to a mistaken idea or failed plan. Cambodia has unfortunate experience with those who were utterly dedicated to a deadly and failed ideology. Commitment doesn’t prove a vision correct. But a lack of commitment and dedication shows clearly that this vision, right or wrong, will never come to pass . Let’s think of a young boy who wants to be a Picasso or a Rembrandt. The young painter dreams of becoming an artist so one day he goes to his father with his dream. “May I become an artist?” His father booms adamantly, “No!” The son persists, refusing to be discouraged. 77 The father relents, but just a little. “Listen to me, Son. You will never become an artist unless you feel you can do nothing else. If you have even an inkling of doing something else, do that, whatever it is. If you want fame, fortune, success or reputation, don’t even consider becoming an artist. If you think you need your father’s approval to become an artist, you have already failed to become one. On the other hand, if becoming an artist consumes your bones so much that you can think of nothing else, become an artist. If your every dream is filled with art and in your every waking moment, you think of becoming an artist, then chase your dream. But if you decide to chase that dream, you must never, ever turn back. You must make a lifetime commitment at that very moment. Otherwise, you will have already failed before you have even started.” Let’s think, for a moment, of another example, of a Japanese sumo wrestler who dreams of being a grand champion. In Japan, future sumo wrestlers enter the sumo world at the age of 15. They do not attend high school which in Japan means that they have given up all job prospects and employability outside of the sumo world. They have chosen to risk everything on the infinitesimal chance of being a sumo wrestler. On the exceedingly unlikely chance of making a name for themselves. What are the odds that out of the thousands of wrestlers, each with the same dream, they will be the one to wear the twisted rope of a grand champion, a yokozuna. They are trying for the impossible and leaving behind the logical. 78

searchIndex.title: Chapter 5 The Reluctant CEO “The desire to be a politician should bar you for life from ever becoming one
searchIndex.text: As a new sumo recruit, they are treated to endless hazing and indignation. Forced to wake up at 4:00AM, clean the practice area, cook breakfast for the higher ranked wrestlers and then only be allowed to eat what little might remain after everyone else has finished eating. They are never called by name, only summoned by grunts, sent on endless errands, even forced to wipe the backsides of higher ranked wrestlers in some extreme cases. Everything in the sumo regimen is designed to break their spirits and make them give up. Or to hone them into absolute single-minded addiction to and obsession with their dreams. Many do the former. They give up and retreat under the intense pressure. But a few refuse to give up their dreams. After all, they didn’t choose sumo. Sumo chose them. All in, for a one in a million chance of becoming a superstar. If they don’t make a name for themselves, they will spend their lives working in a sumo restaurant as a dishwasher or perhaps working as a janitor in a sumo stable or a sumo barber or as cleaning staff at the sumo arena. Demeaning, draining jobs with limited pay. And yet, fully aware of this harsh reality, they still give up everything for their dream. The dream that so rarely comes true. Why? Because the dream compels them and they have no choice but to follow that dream. 79 How far are you willing to go for your dreams? That mindset of the young artist or the sumo wrestler is the same mindset of dedication that pushed Phally to start VP.Start. To take the risk that only has a one in a million chance of success. To jump off the cliff even though everyone says he would never survive the fall. That is the power that helped him and his dedicated team create the first DRC prototypes, the first humble attempt to create plug and play solutions to revolutionize the electric grid while using its existing infrastructure. Previously, there had always been a conundrum, an unsolvable catch 22 to the grid modernization in Cambodia. And across the developing world. Grid modernization was imperative to gain international investment but without international investment, grid modernization was impossibly expensive. A complete overhaul of the entire electric grid was needed but no such funds existed . The only way to raise that kind of starting capital would be to get massive investment, but without a viable electric grid, there was no way to garner investment more than a trickle. How do you transform a bottleneck into an opportunity? How do you change the way you view things with positive thinking? The genius of the DRC technology was to see this impasse as an opportunity . If it were simply impossible to get the revenue required to revamp and rebuild the electric grid from scratch, 80

searchIndex.title: Chapter 5 The Reluctant CEO “The desire to be a politician should bar you for life from ever becoming one
searchIndex.text: VP.Start decided that they must find a way to modernize the grid by leveraging the aging infrastructure already available. Furthermore, if they could succeed in this, they would provide a blueprint for any of the many, many other developing countries which similarly needed comprehensive grid modernization but similarly lacked funds to achieve the transformation. The DRC concept is deceptively simple. The technology gathers data from the electric transmission lines regularly and uses that data to spot anomalies and potential outages before they happen. The “R” of the DRC is “remote” meaning that this data is collected and visualized at a control room using the SCADA system, the RPM Grid. In other words, the entire system is monitored remotely , potential issues are noted remotely and then solutions are applied, most of the time, remotely as well. Recently in Phnom Penh, a new airport has just been opened in a still, as this is being written, undeveloped farming area. As a results, the air traffic tower is visible at quite a distance and has become something of a tourist attraction for locals. The SCADA system of the power grid is similar in function to the air traffic tower, overseeing and monitoring from on high, making decisions, changing routes and avoiding problems in real-time . If we stick with this metaphor, the DRC might be like the radars that provide the data to enable the air traffic controllers to make decisions accurately, promptly and efficiently. 81 Change your thinking. Change your solutions. Change the grid. Change the world. The DRC brought state of the art, cutting edge technology to a place where it was affordable and accessible. A single DRC unit could be manufactured by VP.Start for a very limited price and then sold to utilities and electric licensees for a handsome profit. These DRC units would then provide significant reductions in energy waste, outages, and leakages while promoting energy efficiency and eliminating redundant work. Soon, EDC was on board as were more than a 100 other customers. VP.Start had only just been founded in 2014 and yet the grid modernization revolution was well under way in 2015, even before VP.Start had become an officially registered company. In the very early days, the few members of the VP.Start all wore several hats and headed several departments. Everyone did research and development, everyone did marketing, everyone did testing and quality control, everyone did customer service. This experience would serve the company later as it started to diversify and grow. The leadership knew the challenges and details of every aspect of the entire VP.Start project. This is one reason that VP.Start has always insisted on agility and decentralized management.
